examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
List operations depend on which pointers are available. Deleting a known node in a doubly linked list is constant-time, but finding its position still costs traversal. A singly linked tail needs its predecessor for ordinary deletion. Relink before freeing and preserve the next pointer if continuing traversal. Deleting consecutive matches requires rechecking the new successor rather than advancing the predecessor too early.

**Key relationship:** Insert after p: new.next=p.next; p.next=new

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. Record head, tail and available predecessors.
2. Update links in a safe order.
3. Test empty, single-node and consecutive-match cases.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: For deletion, identify whether a predecessor is available and handle head/tail cases. Given only a node in a singly linked list, deleting the tail still requires finding its predecessor. A loop testing current->next never examines the original head. After removal, keep the predecessor in place to catch consecutive matches.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
In list 1→2→2→3, retain the head and repeatedly delete its current successor when that successor is 2. How many reachable nodes remain?

**Answer: 2.** Remove the first 2 after head 1, then inspect the new successor and remove the second 2. Retain 3. The final list is 1→3, with two nodes.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
Unlinking does not automatically free memory. A production deletion routine must manage ownership and update external head/tail pointers.

Constant-time insertion assumes the insertion position is already known; finding it can cost Θ(n).

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

Deleting a singly linked tail given only head generally costs:

- **A.** O(log n)
- **B.** O(n)
- **C.** O(n²)
- **D.** O(1)

**Answer: B.** Find the predecessor by traversal before changing its next pointer. A head pointer alone does not supply it.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Choose true statements.

- **A.** A doubly linked node has predecessor/successor links
- **B.** Finding an arbitrary key may take linear time
- **C.** Unlinking automatically frees C heap memory
- **D.** Deleting head can require changing the external head pointer

**Answer: A, B, D.** Unlinking and deallocation are separate operations; C does not automatically free removed nodes.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

List 1→2→2→2→3 removes every node whose value is 2. Remaining node count?



**Answer: 2.** All three matching nodes are unlinked, leaving 1→3 and two reachable nodes.

#### Pattern 4 · NAT · Transfer problem

List 2→2→3→2→4 is processed by retaining its head and repeatedly deleting current->next if that successor has value 2, otherwise advancing current. Reachable nodes at the end?



**Answer: 3.** The original head is never inspected for deletion. Remove its matching successor, retain 3, then remove the 2 following 3. Final list is 2→3→4, containing three nodes.

examGuide.title: Work through the supplied PYQs
examGuide.body:
#### GATE 2025 CS1 · Q62 · NAT

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/linked-lists?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Singly and doubly linked lists. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. The loop tests ptr1->next, so the first node of L1 is never considered for deletion. Each later node is removed if its value occurs anywhere in L2.
2. From L1=[1,7,12,3,9,5,11,15,8], it removes 12,9,11,15. It retains the head 1 even though 1 occurs in L2.
3. The remaining reachable list is [1,7,3,5,8], with **5 nodes**. Unlinking is not the same as freeing memory.

#### GATE 2023 CS · Q13 · MCQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/linked-lists?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Singly and doubly linked lists. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. Deleting the tail of a singly linked list requires finding its predecessor from the head. A pointer to the tail alone cannot perform the usual successor-copy trick. Worst case: O(n).
2. A doubly linked node has a predecessor pointer, so its neighbours and the head can be updated in O(1), including boundary cases.
3. Hence **D**: SLLdel O(n), DLLdel O(1).
